text: How does an artificial intelligence actually understand what a word means using nothing but math?
You might already know that before an AI can read text, it breaks words down into tokens
and assigns each one a unique number called a token ID.
This graphic shows four student ID numbers. If you know a student's ID, it might let them
into the building, but it is just an identifier. The number doesn't tell you anything about
their personality. It won't tell you if they are funny, play hockey, or steal fries at lunch.
Token IDs work exactly the same way. They identify a piece of text, but they don't describe it.
Because an identifier only identifies, AI models require an entirely different system of numbers
to actually capture definitions and descriptions. This chart maps a taste test for Coke and coffee.
Rating six characteristics from 0 to 10, Coke scores high on sweet and fizz,
while coffee scores higher on bitter, heat, and caffeine. The entire row of numbers is a vector.
Each trait is a dimension, and the specific number is its value. If asked which drink scores
9 for sweet and 10 for fizz, you wouldn't need to guess. You know immediately it is Coke.
You have just used an ordered row of numbers as a precise mathematical profile for a real-world
item. Introducing a third drink, Pepsi, creates a problem. Looking at the original six dimensions,
Pepsi scores exactly the same as Coke. The data cannot tell them apart. To separate them,
we add a seventh dimension, citrus. Now we see a difference. Coke scores a 1, while Pepsi scores
a 10. When meanings overlap, adding a new mathematical dimension allows the profile to
capture subtle differences that the earlier metrics completely missed. This table compares
our simple taste test to how an AI builds internal profiles. Instead of three drinks,
the AI evaluates every token in its vocabulary across thousands of dimensions.
While we chose simple numbers, the AI independently learns complex,
positive, negative, and decimal numbers. Importantly, these dimensions don't have
human labels. They capture abstract patterns in token usage. Despite the massive scale
and the lack of familiar labels, the underlying mechanism is identical.
Both systems use an ordered row of numbers to mathematically describe what something is.
Let's bring all this together and look at a diagram of a real embedding table.
When you type the word CAT into an AI, here is exactly what happens mathematically.
First, the text CAT is converted to its token ID, in this case 4719. The system uses that
number as a lookup address to find its specific row in the table. Inside that row, the columns
marked D1, D2, and so on represent the abstract dimensions. Each position holds a specific
completely assembled row of learned numbers, you're looking at the token's embedding.
This system is so robust that even fragments of words get their own profiles. If you input
unbelievable, the AI splits it into UN, BELIE, and VABEL, and each of those fragments receives
its own unique embedding. AI uses numbers to work with meaning. Those numbers help
AI recognize similarities and differences.
